issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette:
Carlos was sixty-one years old, a modern dance instructor who had spent four decades shaping students with the same disciplined grace he had once brought to the stage. That night, driving home from a late rehearsal, he was stopped at an intersection when a pickup truck blew through the red light and slammed into the driver's side of his sedan. He remembers the sound more than the sight: the screech of tires, the explosive pop of metal crumpling, then the long, grinding scrape as his car spun. After that, silence, except for the hiss of a leaking radiator and his own ragged breathing. He was pinned for twenty minutes before emergency crews cut him free. He had not been severely injured physically, but something in him had been torn loose.

In the weeks that followed, Carlos found he could not put what had happened into words. When his wife, Elena, asked him about it, he would shrug or turn away-not from unwillingness, but because the event lived in him as a jumble of sounds and sensations, not a story he could tell. Sometimes, without warning, he would hear the screech of tires again, so vivid that he would flinch and look around, certain the crash was about to replay. Those moments left him soaked in a shame he could not explain: a conviction that the accident had happened because of the sort of person he was-careless, distracted, undeserving of good fortune. He started to believe that he would never feel normal emotions again, that the part of him that had once laughed easily and felt joy had been crushed in the wreck. A deeper helplessness settled in: he could not stop bad things from happening, so why bother trying?

His behavior shifted quietly at first. He began staying up until two or three in the morning, scrolling his phone or staring at the ceiling, because the moment he closed his eyes the sounds would start, and with them the shame. During the day, when a memory surfaced or a stressful moment arose, he would deliberately try to blank out-closing his eyes, going numb, leaving his body as if stepping behind a thick glass wall. He worked hard to suppress any thoughts of the crash, but the harder he pushed them away, the more the sounds ambushed him. He came to dread being touched unexpectedly; Elena's hand on his shoulder could make him jerk away with a surge of alarm, and he would see the hurt in her face before he could explain. He started scanning every room he entered for exits, noting doors and windows automatically, even in his own home. In the dance studio, where he taught modern technique, the mirrors that once helped him refine his form now made him hyperaware of potential escape routes, and the accidental brush of a student's hand during a partnering exercise sent his heart racing. The age he wore-the slight stiffness in his knees, the careful way he rose from a chair-now felt like a liability, as if his body had become something fragile that could break again at any moment.

The consequences crept into his marriage and his work. Carlos began arriving late to rehearsals, claiming fatigue, then canceling classes because he felt too "off." Elena, who had always been his softest landing, grew quietly distant; she did not know how to reach him when even a gentle touch startled him. He was haunted by the thought that he was failing her, failing his students, failing himself-and that this failure was simply another proof of his unworthiness. What finally drove him to seek help was a morning when he could not bring himself to unlock the studio door. He stood in the parking lot, scanning the exits, and knew he could not go in. He called a therapist from his car, his voice trembling. He was afraid of what he would find-afraid he would learn that he truly had lost his emotions forever, that the shame was deserved, that at sixty-one he was too old to rebuild-but he was also desperately hoping that somewhere inside him, the dancer who felt music in his bones was still there, waiting to be touched again.
